items_missed: No upfront agenda statement and no timeframe. The roadmap came at minute ~10, after the entire probe: 'let me walk you through how our pricing is gonna work and then I'll go over your estimate specifically for you.' Good language, wrong place — the customer sat through a long inventory interview with no idea how long it would take or what was coming. No '10-15 minutes' framing anywhere.

Never asked 'how are you today?' The customer opened by telling him she had been on hold six minutes and got dumped to voicemail. He apologized ('I'm sorry that you got placed on hold... I had left the office to go pick up a truck from the shop') but never turned it into a check-in on her.

Never asked the moving-stressor question. This customer handed him the answer unprompted — she volunteered that she is 81 ('I'm not probably gonna be doing a whole lot of packing') and that a previous mover refused her extra boxes on move day ('they wouldn't take them. I had to call somebody at the last minute'). He answered the box fear well but never asked 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?', so he found the stressor by luck rather than by process.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. 'Insurance' appeared only as a line item inside the hourly rate — 'the truck gas taxes insurance' — with zero explanation of the $2,000 per-move repair/replace/reimburse coverage. This on a call where the customer walked him through artwork, a glass-door TV console, a wicker swing chair on a metal stand, and a drop-leaf table, and said 'I think it's safe in a box.'
Meet Your Mover never mentioned. No reference to the pre-move email with the mover's photo — a natural fit for an 81-year-old customer letting a two-man crew into her house for two consecutive days.
No 60c/lb baseline. The full insurance explanation (No Worries plus the legal baseline) never happened, so the customer has no idea what coverage she actually has.

No consolidation examples and no 'take a carload' tip. The Save Your Ass content only appeared reactively, when she asked 'if I have boxes packed they can go to, right?' and he answered 'whatever you pack before we get there, we'll just make this cheaper and quicker for you.' True, but nothing about loose items in drawers, photos off walls, garden tools, or small stuff in the car — and she is actively deciding what to take, which is exactly when those tips land.

No booking attempt. This is the biggest miss on the call. He got a yes on the two-day structure ('we could come out on maybe Wednesday the thirtieth to pack... and then on Thursday the first to actually move it. Is that something you'd be okay with?' / 'Yes.') and then never asked for the business. When she said 'I've got a couple of quotes so I'll just review them and... I think I've got three quotes right now,' he answered 'Of course, I totally understand' and pivoted to no-deposit. No 'want me to hold the 30th and 1st for you?', no follow-up date set, no next-step commitment on a comparison-shopping customer who had already agreed to the dates.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections.' He said 'answer the questions that are at the bottom of the quote' — that is a booking instruction, not an ask to verify the details, which matters here because the inventory was unusually complicated (partial bedrooms, no bedroom furniture, no coffee table, no TV).
Hours and how to reach us not given. Only 'just call us back at this number here.' No office hours.

Drive time never explained as a time variable. The customer volunteered 'somewhere between seven and eight miles' and he never told her the drive counts on the clock, or whether Arlington sits inside the Fort Worth service zone (no trip fee was quoted either way).

Estimate delivery was internally inconsistent and reads padded. He said 'about six and a half maybe seven and a half hours on each day on the first day' and then 'both days, about seven and a half hours' in the same breath, and priced off 7.5. He had just told her a full 1200 sqft move runs 'seven to eight hours for two guys' — but this move drops all bedroom furniture, the coffee table, and the TV. Quoting the top of the full-home range on a stripped-down inventory is the conservative-manager pattern, and it inflated the $3,185 number the customer is now comparing against two other bids.

He was never clearly identified. His name came through in a mangled greeting ('Good morning or good afternoon biggest now Jenny, this is grant with Einstein Moving Company com') and at the 19-minute mark she asked 'what was your name again? Frank.' He recovered ('My name is grant. My name is grant. That'll be in the email') but a customer who cannot name her rep is a weaker referral and a weaker callback.
top_strength: The probe and the pricing block were near-textbook, and the recovery was better. He inherited an annoyed customer — six minutes on hold, then a voicemail prompt — and turned it around inside two exchanges by owning it plainly ('I'm sorry that you got placed on hold. I had left the office to go pick up a truck from the shop') and then riffing on her own joke about the hold music ('I'm glad that at least it was somewhat pleasant six minutes'). From there the discovery was genuinely thorough: origin and destination addresses with zips, square footage at both ends, room-by-room inventory including the partial-bedroom nuance ('So we really aren't moving any bedroom furniture at all'), garage and backyard, appliances, gun safes and workout equipment, fragile items, parking and walk distance at BOTH locations, third floor plus elevator, and whether the elevator can be reserved. He caught the access wrinkle she raised and logged it out loud: 'I'll just put access might be a little tricky for us.' The pricing section hit almost every bullet verbatim — 'pricing is super simple on Wednesdays and Thursdays. We charge $97 per hour per mover... So that'd be $194 an hour. Everything is included in that hourly rate? So the truck gas taxes insurance, all of the pads wrap and bands... and then any tools needed for disassemble or reassembly' — followed by a clean no-hidden-fees pitch, the full clock explanation (starts on arrival with the walkthrough, 2.5-hour minimum, 15-minute prorated increments), a sense-check, the On-Time Guarantee, and no-deposit plus no cancellation fee. His handling of her one real objection was the best moment on the call: instead of a generic reassurance about extra boxes he gave her the capacity equivalent and a plan — 'our box trucks they're 26 footers. They can hold the content of about a fully furnished seventeen to 1800 square foot home... If you start creeping into maybe triple digits give me a call let me know and we can allocate maybe a third person.' He also framed budget honestly and repeatedly: 'if it ends up taking less time than what I've quoted you, it'll end up being cheaper for you at the end of the day.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: he built the whole sale and then walked away from the close. She had already said yes to the 30th and the 1st. The moment she said 'I've got three quotes right now and let me stop there,' the line was: 'Totally fair, Jinny — and here's the easy part. There's no deposit and no cancellation fee, so let me put the 30th and the 1st on the schedule right now while they're open. If one of the other quotes wins, you call me and I take you off, no charge. That way you're not comparison shopping against a calendar that's filling up.' That is a zero-risk ask he had already earned, and he had every ingredient in hand — he even delivered the no-deposit and no-cancellation-fee lines thirty seconds later, just as a parting reassurance instead of as the close. Second priority: if he isn't going to book it, book the follow-up. He ended on 'just call us back at this number here' and put the next move entirely on an 81-year-old customer holding three bids. He should have said 'I'll give you a call Tuesday to see where you landed — does late morning work?' Third: No Worries Damage Coverage is missing from a call where she inventoried artwork, glass cabinet doors, and a wicker swing chair. When she said 'I think the artwork is pretty. I think it's safe in a box,' the answer was 'Good — and either way you're covered. Our No Worries Damage Coverage covers up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse anything we accidentally damage, and it's included, not an add-on.' Pair that with Meet Your Mover, which is a two-second add and disproportionately reassuring for a solo senior customer hosting a crew two days running. Fourth, and this one is Amanda's rock, not just Grant's: the estimate math. 7.5 hours priced at the very top of his own stated 'seven to eight hours' range for a FULL 1200 sqft home, on a move with no bedroom furniture, no coffee table, and no TV, is padding — and he said the quiet part out loud: 'since we don't know how long the walk is at the unload location I'm gonna play it safe with the estimate and just kind of air on the side of caution.' The disclosure is honest and the hourly model protects her, but a $3,185 number going up against two other bids can lose a job it should have won. The better move is to quote the realistic middle (6.5 on the move day given the reduced inventory), name the unload walk as the one variable, and tell her exactly what would push it up. Last, small but real: fix the opener so the customer catches his name. Nineteen minutes in she asked 'what was your name again? Frank.' A clean 'Hi Jinny, this is Grant with Einstein Moving Company' plus the agenda statement up front fixes both the name problem and the missing roadmap in one sentence.
phone_presence_notes: He converted an irritated customer into a chatty one through real rapport — owning the six-minute hold, joking about the smoker ('No, like, 500 gallon smokers or anything like that. Nothing crazy back there'), following her Lockheed tangent ('I have a friend that works with them right now'), heavy natural name use, and a warm close she reciprocated with 'Thank you so much' — held back from a 5 only by never asking how she was doing and by her not retaining his name.
